request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis: Every fit so far fails badly. The residual RMS is about 1.0e5 arcsec (~29 deg), and the noise sigma was simply fitted to that same value. Mean east residuals drift monotonically with time from -6.9e4 to +9.9e4 arcsec, and the first time bin has an RMS of 3e5 arcsec. Fitting an ellipse to each half of the arc gives very different periods (4125 vs 11990 d) and a large apsidal shift of about 95 deg/orbit. Together this points to a strongly non-Keplerian force over 5–12 AU, not small perturbations. The power law is best but leaves enormous structure; its low C and n≈2.2 may reflect a poor local optimum. Proposed next: Newton plus an extra term that grows relative to gravity with distance (Hooke-like or constant), and Newton plus an unseen perturbing planet.

proposals.rationale: An extra linear term (halo or cosmological-constant-like) changes the force strongly between 5 and 12 AU. This produces large apsidal precession and different apparent periods in the inner and outer parts of the orbit.
A constant radial acceleration (MOND-like or Pioneer-like) dominates more at large r. It is an alternative to the Hooke term with the same single parameter.
Tests whether a massive unseen planet, rather than a modified central law, causes the precession and the drift in mean motion.
